sources.file: (K) The Road Goes Ever On - A Song Cycle.pdf
sources.attribution: J.R.R. Tolkien, music Donald Swann (1967; 2nd ed. 1978)
sources.note: THE MOST WANTED OF THE ABSENT, because the archive ALREADY CITES IT: The War of the Jewels refers the reader to 'The Road Goes Ever On, p. 61' for miruvórë, so the corpus depends on a book it does not hold. Published in Tolkien's lifetime and carrying his own commentary on Namárië and A Elbereth Gilthoniel -- the only place he glossed those two texts word by word. ARRIVED 2026-07-30 AND IS AN IMAGE-ONLY SCAN, 78pp with no text layer. The dependency this row was written about is therefore NOT resolved: the corpus still cites 'The Road Goes Ever On, p. 61' for miruvórë. Held. EXTRACTION: OCR-DERIVED TEXT NOW EXISTS -- two independent digitisations, tesseract-read from the image-only scan and searchable (corpus/t1_ocr_k_the_road_goes_ever_on_a_song_cycle.txt, 23,035 words; a second digitisation, 12,168 words), but not checked against the plate and not a quotation until it is. A direct search for 'miruvórë' did not resolve in either OCR file, which may be an OCR/accent-normalisation gap rather than an absence -- the dependency this row was written about is not yet confirmed resolved, only no longer silently unreadable.
sources.digitisation_of: The Road Goes Ever On - A Song Cycle (J.R.R. Tolkien & Donald Swann, 1967)
sources.digitisation_note: Two scans of one 1967 songbook. Recorded as a pair because the attributions register and attrib_check both assume one text per book: without this, a quotation found in both verifies 'in exactly two books' and is one book counted twice. NEITHER COPY IS A RELIABLE WITNESS TO THE ELVISH. Scored against Namárië as printed in The Lord of the Rings, over 28 distinctive Quenya forms: folded, the OCR holds 23 and this second scan 16; exactly accented, 6 and 8. The OCR drops diacritics and sometimes invents them (`tellumar` read as `téllumar`); the second misreads letters outright (`miruvórë` read as `miruvére`), its pages being musical scores. Neither holds one correctly accented form of Namárië's Quenya, so the citation this volume was sought for — The War of the Jewels sending the reader to p. 61 for `miruvórë` — cannot be followed from either.
sources.text_provenance_note: Machine-read by map/ocr_campaign.py on 31 July 2026 at 300 dpi greyscale with tesseract -l Latin, then accent-restored against the archive's clean corpus and the Eldamo lexicon. Measured against a known-good text of Vinyar Tengwar 39: 93% of accented forms correct, conditioned on the word being read. NOT a publisher's text layer; nothing here is a quotation until a reader has checked it against the plate.

sources.file: The Art of The Lord of the Rings.pdf
sources.attribution: ed. Gary Russell / the film design team (New Line, 2002-04) -- NOT Hammond & Scull
sources.note: LICENSED FILM CONCEPT ART, AND I FILED IT FOR THREE WEEKS AS TOLKIEN'S OWN HAND. The owner caught it and was right to ask whether I had read what he sent. I had not: I matched the TITLE against Hammond & Scull's 2015 book of Tolkien's own drawings for The Lord of the Rings, and wrote an attribution, a tier and a note from that assumption. THE FILE IS A DIFFERENT BOOK. Its own opening says so in the first forty words -- it describes filming the Lord of the Rings trilogy, teams of artists and designers turning that vision into moviemaking magic, Academy Awards and BAFTA, and sketches, conceptual art, sculptures and digital paintings selected by the artists themselves. Measured after the OCR: 139 occurrences of film vocabulary, against 29 in the Companion and Guide, which discusses the adaptations legitimately, and 0 in every volume of Tolkien's own writing. WHAT THE OLD NOTE ASSERTED WAS WORSE THAN THE WRONG TIER. It said the book carried Tolkien's own working maps and the note-sheets behind them, and that THE GAZETTEER'S COORDINATES WERE MEASURED AGAINST THEM -- a provenance I invented for a film tie-in, in the register that decides which source wins a disagreement. Nothing was ever measured against it and it is in no corpus index, so no coordinate and no quotation rests on it; the damage was a published claim, not a corrupted dataset. TIER 4 BY THE ARCHIVE'S OWN DEFINITION: t3 is for writing and pictures that do not contradict Tolkien and sit in harmony with him, and a film design is an ADAPTATION that contradicts him wherever the films depart from the books. t4 is for what is usable only where Tolkien himself would have owned the claim, which is exactly right for concept art of his world made by other hands. It sits beside The Art of The Fellowship of the Ring, which is the same kind of book and was correctly attributed to Gary Russell from the start -- the two rows now agree.

The mechanism is why it survives its sample: the 2023 edition gives a NEW letter a suffix and leaves an EXPANDED one on its base number, so the suffix IS the property, not a proxy for it. however, is complete, and lists all 508 letters of the revised edition: the 354 of 1981 and 154 added. sources.attribution: J.R.R. Tolkien; illustrated by Pauline Baynes (1990)
sources.note: Tolkien's own poem, and the last he wrote for publication -- so tier 1 without question. EXTRACTION: PLATE-TRANSCRIBED, 17 Aug, and this row previously said the absence was correct. The old reasoning held that the poem's whole value is its exact wording and that tesseract destroys the diacritic-bearing forms a poem is wanted for, so a machine reading would be worse than an honest absence. THE MEASUREMENT WAS RIGHT AND THE CONCLUSION WAS TOO NARROW. Right: run at 300 dpi over Baynes's paintings, tesseract returned `he "ghJay is ended` for `Day is ended` -- every stanza's decorated initial defeats it. Too narrow twice. First, the argument was about a MACHINE reading, and it never considered a reader looking at the plate; all twelve verse plates were read directly, and the tesseract pass kept only as a second opinion. Second, the diacritic argument does not actually reach this poem: THERE IS NOT ONE ACCENTED CHARACTER IN ITS 24 LINES, so the specific destruction measured was of forms this text does not contain. The metrical division is corroborated by the book's own structure rather than assumed -- twelve verse plates in three groups of four, two metrical lines a plate, giving 3 stanzas of 8 and couplet rhyme throughout -- and the printed display layout is preserved plate by plate beneath the poem so the source's own form is not lost. The PDF's own text layer, 12,040 characters, is front matter plus Baynes's `Notes on the Pictures` and carries none of the verse: pages 1-3 and 6-8 return zero characters.

sources.attribution: J.R.R. Tolkien, ed. Humphrey Carpenter with Christopher Tolkien; revised and expanded by Chris Smith and Brian Sibley (2023)
sources.note: EXTRACTION: CORRECTLY EMPTY -- A SECOND DIGITISATION OF A BOOK THE ARCHIVE ALREADY HOLDS, held and deliberately not extracted, and declared so nobody discovers it a third time. Its text IS in the corpus, once, through the EPUB. Extracting it as well made `attrib_check` go from clean to THIRTEEN findings in a single run -- every one an INCOMPLETE WITNESS LIST naming this file -- which would have published one book as two independent attestations. The registered copy is the EPUB; this is a 740-page PDF of the SAME edition. Measured against each other rather than assumed: 308,261 words here against 308,243 in the EPUB -- 18 words apart in three hundred thousand. NEITHER IS RANKED, on the owner's ruling of 31 July about the two Road Goes Ever On scans: naming a preferred digitisation tells a later reader one can be trusted, and nothing here has measured that. The EPUB remains the corpus source because it already is, not because it won.

sources.attribution: J.R.R. Tolkien (manuscript; printed in Sauron Defeated)
sources.note: Tolkien's own calligraphic manuscript of the King's Letter, the discarded epilogue to The Lord of the Rings, in tengwar and in English. IT IS BOTH A TEXT AND A PICTURE and the artwork ruling of 29 July governs the picture: his linework is NOT republished. Held in the workshop as primary evidence the archive may read and measure against, and may never serve. EXTRACTION: CORRECTLY EMPTY — it is a .png, so there is no text layer to fail and none is expected. The extractor now refuses any source that is not a .pdf or .epub, having handed this picture to pdftotext once and put the 0-byte answer in the corpus.
sources.first_publication_basis: READ BY HAND. A MANUSCRIPT, and a manuscript has no publication date until somebody prints it. The register's own attribution says where: 'J.R.R. Tolkien (manuscript; printed in Sauron Defeated)', and the register dates Sauron Defeated 1992 on its own row, corroborated by that volume's imprint 'First published in Great Britain by HarperCollinsPublishers 1992'. First print 1992, nineteen years after his death.

text_held.why: Christopher Tolkien printed the text of this very manuscript, with a transliteration of both its English and its Sindarin, in HoME IX -- and said in the same breath exactly where the tengwar and the transliteration DISAGREE: the English transliteration omits Arathornsson and adds `day` where the tengwar read `the thirty-first of the Stirring`, and `and Arnor, ar Arnor` was added to both tengwar texts and is absent from both transliterations. All three copies are given, at t1_9_sauron_defeated.txt:4573-4630. So the archive is not owed a machine reading of the plate: it holds the Estate's own reading of it, including the variants an OCR pass could not have known were there. The .png remains what it always was -- a picture with no text layer, correctly extracting to nothing.

retrieval.why: nothing readable to read an identifier out of: this row's corpus text is absent or empty, so the held copy cannot be asked where it came from.

sources.note: Words, Phrases and Passages in Various Tongues in The Lord of the Rings — Tolkien's own late commentary on every scrap of Elvish in the book, and the single most important linguistic source outside the Etymologies. THIS REGISTER NAMED IT AS THE CHIEF ABSENCE and it is now held. EXTRACTION: OCR-DERIVED, 123,801 words at 300 dpi, 2026-07-31. The most wanted volume on this shelf is readable at last -- and the archive can now say exactly how far to trust it, because it holds an INDEPENDENT CLEAN CONTROL for this one volume. GIRAUDEAU'S TWO DERIVED INDICES (t3) list 474 distinct Quenya headwords drawn from PE17, each carrying a [PE17:page] citation -- 3,256 citations reaching 176 of these 221 pages. Checking them against the OCR splits exactly along the diacritic: PLAIN FORMS 215 of 364 survive (59.1%); ACCENTED FORMS 10 of 110 (9.1%). A 6.5x difference, measured against somebody else's clean text rather than against my own sample of VT39. Anduril, Elentari, Endore, Finarato, Lorien, Melcore and Poldorea are all listed by Giraudeau and all lost here. SO THE DERIVED INDEX CAN RESCUE THE SOURCE IT WAS DERIVED FROM: he supplies the correct spelling AND the page it stands on, which is a repair route this shelf did not have before both volumes were held. Until that repair is made and checked, this file is commentary and not orthography.

sources.attribution: J.R.R. Tolkien, music Donald Swann (1967) — a second scan supplied by the owner 2026-07-31
sources.note: THE SAME BOOK AS THE (K) COPY ABOVE AND A DIFFERENT DIGITISATION, kept because the two are COMPLEMENTARY RATHER THAN RANKED. The held copy had no text layer at all and was OCR'd on 30 July; this one carries a layer of its own — and that layer is largely garbled MUSICAL NOTATION, because the book is a song cycle and the pages are scores: 'NAMARIE (FAREWELL) / Freely / play bassnotes as written' arrives mixed with `py - @ 2 Ff «`. So it is not the clean publisher's text the archive hoped for. What it does have is Elvish the OCR lost — `yéni` occurs 3 times here and 0 times in the OCR — so where the two digitisations agree a reading is far better evidenced than where one stands alone. That is the same argument as the two scans of Vinyar Tengwar 39, and the owner supplied both pairs on the same instinct.
sources.digitisation_of: The Road Goes Ever On - A Song Cycle (J.R.R. Tolkien & Donald Swann, 1967)
sources.digitisation_note: Two scans of one 1967 songbook. Recorded as a pair because the attributions register and attrib_check both assume one text per book: without this, a quotation found in both verifies 'in exactly two books' and is one book counted twice. not_held.title: Tales from the Perilous Realm (2008 omnibus)
not_held.note: The omnibus of the minor fiction: Roverandom, Farmer Giles of Ham, The Adventures of Tom Bombadil, Smith of Wootton Major and Leaf by Niggle. NOT the tier-3 study by Marjorie Burns whose filename is nearly the same and which this archive does hold. Farmer Giles of Ham and Leaf by Niggle are independently held in full in The Tolkien Reader (corpus/t1_the_tolkien_reader.txt), so what this omnibus alone would still close is its own edition and Roverandom and Smith of Wootton Major.
not_held.affects: It would close its remaining two declared absences (Roverandom, Smith of Wootton Major), which is why it is worth naming separately.

not_held.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight; Pearl; Sir Orfeo (1975 translations)
not_held.attribution: trans. J.R.R. Tolkien, ed. Christopher Tolkien
not_held.note: Tolkien's verse translations from Middle English. Not Middle-earth; they are the clearest surviving evidence of how he heard alliterative metre, which the Lays and the Fall of Arthur both draw on.
not_held.affects: The verse hall, and any claim about Tolkien's metre. The archive currently reasons about his alliterative practice from the legendarium alone.

not_held.title: The Bovadium Fragments (2025)
not_held.attribution: ed. Christopher Tolkien; essay by Richard Ovenden
not_held.note: A previously unpublished satire on the motor-car and the ruin of Oxford, and the last of Christopher Tolkien's presentations of his father's work. No Middle-earth matter.
not_held.affects: Nothing in this archive. Registered for completeness of the tier-1 shelf.

not_held.title: The Fall of Arthur (2013); The Legend of Sigurd and Gudrún (2009); Beowulf: A Translation and Commentary (2014); The Story of Kullervo (2015); The Lay of Aotrou and Itroun (2016)
not_held.note: Tolkien's verse and translations outside the legendarium.
not_held.affects: Nothing directly; useful only for the sources of his imagination.

not_held.title: Roverandom; Mr Bliss; Letters from Father Christmas; Smith of Wootton Major
not_held.note: His other fiction. Smith touches Faery, but none is Middle-earth.

not_held.title: Parma Eldalamberon 12, 16, 18–22 (1995– )
not_held.attribution: ed. Elvish Linguistic Fellowship, by permission of the Tolkien Estate and with Christopher Tolkien's support
not_held.note: MOSTLY ANSWERED ON 2026-07-30, AND THIS ENTRY IS THE RECORD OF WHAT IT ASKED FOR. It used to name PE 11, 12, 13, 17, 18, 19 and 22 as the single largest body of primary Tolkien not held. Numbers 11, 13, 14, 15, 17 and 23 have since arrived and are registered above — so the Gnomish Lexicon, Early Noldorin and 'Words, Phrases and Passages' are on the shelf. STILL NOT HELD: the Qenya Lexicon (PE 12) and the Quenya phonology and verb structure (PE 16, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22). Giraudeau's derived lexicons at tier 3 give partial access to 12 and 21 and are not a substitute for either. The distinction this entry drew before the volumes came is still the important one: the five issues that arrived on 2026-07-24 are Volume 1, numbers 1-5, the 1971-74 fanzine of the Mythopoeic Linguistic Fellowship containing no Tolkien manuscript, and they remain at tier 3. That is a different publication under the same name. The modern series' text is Tolkien's and carries tier-1 authority; the journals are the Estate-permitted vehicle.
not_held.affects: The languages hall above all. Its lexicon is built from the Etymologies (HoME V) and the published appendices; PE 22 would correct and greatly enlarge it. Until it is read, no entry in that hall should be presented as the whole of what Tolkien wrote.

not_held.title: Vinyar Tengwar — every issue except 11, 12, 14, 24, 25, 27, 28, 29, 31, 36, 37, 39, 41, 43 and the combined 41–50 volume (so 13 IS missing, which the old range hid)
not_held.attribution: ed. Elvish Linguistic Fellowship, by Estate permission
not_held.note: LARGELY ANSWERED ON 2026-07-30. This entry asked for 'Ósanwe-kenta', 'Notes on Óre', 'The Rivers and Beacon-hills of Gondor' and the Quenya prayers, and all four are now held: nos. 41-50 arrived as one 404-page volume of clean text, and Ósanwe-kenta as a clean extract of no. 39. WHAT IS HELD IS NOT THE SAME AS WHAT IS READABLE, and for this run the gap is wide: of the twenty-two issues now on the shelf, ELEVEN ARE IMAGE-ONLY SCANS and TWO MORE carry OCR so corrupt it must not be extracted. Readable today: nos. 41-50, no. 43, and the Ósanwe-kenta extract. Still not held at all: the issues below 11, and 15-23, 26, 30, 32-35, 38, 40.
not_held.affects: The languages hall; also the cosmology and any statement about Elvish mind and spirit.

not_held.title: The Art of The Lord of the Rings (2015)
not_held.note: Tolkien's own drawings, maps and designs for The Lord of the Rings, reproduced in full. ITS COMPANION, The Art of The Hobbit, ARRIVED 2026-07-30 and is registered above — OCR-derived text now exists for its captions (26,107 words, tesseract-read), though not yet checked against the plate.
not_held.affects: The gallery and the maps. His own cartography outranks any reconstruction the archive draws. Wanted for the captions and datings; under the artwork ruling the plates are not republished.

not_held.title: Tolkien: Maker of Middle-earth (2018)
not_held.note: The exhibition catalogue: manuscripts, letters and artwork, including heraldic devices.

not_held.title: The Hobbit: Graphic Novel — new edition (September 2026)
not_held.attribution: adapted by Chuck Dixon and Sean Deming; illustrated by David Wenzel; first published 1989-90
not_held.note: An authorised adaptation, not a source. Its text is Tolkien's story abridged into panels and its pictures are Wenzel's reading of it, so nothing in it can settle a question of fact: where it differs from The Hobbit, The Hobbit wins. Tiered 3 by the user's judgement on 2026-07-24 — licensed by the Estate, which would argue for tier 2, but the tier records what a source IS, and an adaptation stands beside Fonstad's atlas rather than beside a published text.
not_held.affects: Nothing in this archive rests on it, and nothing should. Of interest only to the gallery, as one more record of how the tale has been visualised — and there it would be cited as Wenzel's art, never as evidence for how anything in Middle-earth looked.

retrieval_summary.what: Whether each source in this register can be retrieved by somebody who is not this archive. `path` means an identifier read out of the copy we hold -- an ISBN from its copyright page, an ISSN from its masthead, the address a saved web page prints of itself. `unrecorded` means no such identifier is printed in our copy and nobody has looked one up. Nothing here is guessed: an invented ISBN would look checkable and be false, which is worse than an empty field.
retrieval_summary.granularity: `item` reaches this exact thing. `serial` reaches the periodical it belongs to, and the row's own title names the issue.

rule: Where two sources disagree, the lower tier number wins. A tier-5 file is corrected by any tier above it. Tolkien's own words quoted inside a tier-2 book carry tier-1 authority; the editor's framing does not.

limits.what: The genealogical tables of Appendix A III (Durin's Folk) and Appendix C (the hobbit trees)
limits.why: In the edition held here these tables are embedded as IMAGES, not text, so no text extraction reaches them. They have now been recovered by rendering the pages and reading the plates directly, and cross-checked with tesseract OCR.
limits.effect: RESOLVED. The Dwarf line is verified against App A III: six birth-years were wrong in this archive and are corrected (Nain I was out by 101 years). The hobbit dates are verified against App C and were correct in every case checked, but now carry the warrant they lacked. Where OCR and a direct reading disagreed, the reading was confirmed at 450 dpi and OCR was found to be the one in error.

resolved_absences.title: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien — Revised and Expanded Edition (2023), letters 43-354 and 40a onward
resolved_absences.attribution: ed. Carpenter & C. Tolkien; revised Hammond & Scull
resolved_absences.closed_by: the owner supplied the complete Revised and Expanded Edition as a PDF with a real text layer. Extracted with pdftotext -enc UTF-8 and MEASURED before it replaced the excerpt: 308,261 words against the excerpt's 36,185, a gain of 8.5x; 351 distinct letter headers spanning 1 to 354, against the excerpt's 42; 740 control characters in 1,706,988, which is 0.04% and is a real text layer rather than OCR.
resolved_absences.note: THIS WAS THE ARCHIVE'S FIRST DECLARED ABSENCE and it stood from 2026-07-24. Two standing restrictions fall with it: the archive may now QUOTE the whole edition rather than only letters 1-42, and it may no longer treat 'absent from the Letters' as unanswerable -- a search that finds nothing in this volume is now evidence rather than a gap in the shelf.

was.title: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien — Revised and Expanded Edition (2023), letters 43-354 and 40a onward
was.attribution: ed. Carpenter & C. Tolkien; revised Hammond & Scull
was.note: PARTLY HELD as of 2026-07-24. The excerpt now on the shelf gives the complete contents list — 508 letters, the 354 of 1981 plus 154 added — and the full text of letters 1 to 42, including thirteen that 1981 never printed. What is still missing is the text of the remaining 141 new letters, and the passages the revision restored to letters 43-354.
was.affects: The archive may now name which letters exist, to whom and when, for the whole edition. It may quote only 1-42 from the revision, and must otherwise cite the 1981 text. It still may not assert that a subject is absent from the Letters.

resolved_absences.title: The Monsters and the Critics and Other Essays (1983)
resolved_absences.closed_by: Measured against the shelf rather than assumed: corpus/t1_the_monsters_and_the_critics_and_other_essays.txt holds 105,074 words, and the two essays this entry said were 'still wanted' — 'On Fairy-Stories' and 'English and Welsh' — both verify present with map/ardatext.py's folding matcher, as do 'A Secret Vice' and the 'Valedictory Address'.
resolved_absences.note: THE ABSENCE WAS FALSE, AND A FALSE ABSENCE IS THE MIRROR OF A FALSE SILENCE: it hides the archive's own evidence from it and tells a reader to stop looking. Any page that hedged on Tolkien's philosophy of invention for want of these essays is now revisitable — the archive may quote them.

supersedes.note: TWO EDITIONS OF ONE BOOK, not two books. The 2023 revision is the CITATION OF RECORD; the 1981 text stays on the shelf as a WITNESS to what the revision changed, which is a different question from what Tolkien wrote. Declared 12 Aug because attrib_check went red the hour the complete edition landed: five spans bound to 1981 began verifying in the revision too, both tier 1, and the guard read that as a choice among rival sources. It is not one, and the hierarchy is not the only thing that speaks here. ANY better edition of a book already held will produce that finding once per shared passage, so this is a data row rather than a special case in a guard.
